clinicalPearls: A. fumigatus causes most invasive aspergillosis, >95% of chronic aspergillosis, and most allergic syndromes; only species that grow at 37C cause invasive infection (Harrison 22e p.1713)

The disease spectrum spans three categories: invasive (acute/subacute in the immunocompromised), chronic/saprophytic (chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma/fungal ball), and allergic (ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis) (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1714)

Invasive aspergillosis is one of the most common diagnostic errors revealed at autopsy; keys to early diagnosis are a high index of suspicion, circulating antigen screening (in leukemia), and urgent thoracic CT (Harrison 22e p.1714)

On thoracic CT the halo sign (ground-glass hemorrhagic infarction around a nodule/consolidation) appears for ~7 days early in neutropenic patients and is a good prognostic feature reflecting early diagnosis; the air-crescent/cavitation appears later (Harrison 22e p.1716)

Galactomannan antigen detection on respiratory samples (e.g., tracheobronchial/BAL fluid) is more sensitive than serum and is critical in ventilated/ICU patients where radiology is nonspecific; positive serum antigen usually precedes clinical or radiologic features by several days (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1716)

Antigen, beta-D-glucan, and real-time PCR are faster and far more sensitive than culture, as only 10-30% of invasive aspergillosis cases yield a positive culture; antifungal therapy reduces antigen sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1716)

Aspergillus IgG antibody is detectable in ~90% of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and ~65% of Aspergillus nodules; ABPA is diagnosed by Aspergillus-specific IgE (or positive skin-prick test) plus elevated total IgE, usually >1000 IU/mL (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1715)

Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis follows pulmonary tuberculosis in ~6-13% of treated cases and is often initially mistaken for tuberculosis; >90% of chronic cavitary cases occur in patients with prior lung disease (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1715)

On tissue histology Aspergillus hyphae are hyaline, narrow, and septate with branching at 45 degrees; angioinvasion with vascular invasion by hyphae is characteristic in neutropenia (Harrison 22e p.1716)

HEPA filtration is often protective and should be installed and monitored in operating rooms, burn units, and areas housing high-risk patients; hospital outbreaks usually relate to a contaminated air source or construction (Harrison 22e p.1713)
harrison.pathophysiology: Aspergillus is a ubiquitous hyaline septate branching mold whose conidia (spores) are inhaled from indoor/outdoor air; only species growing at 37C cause invasive disease. Disease form depends on host immunity. Invasive disease arises with profound neutropenia, glucocorticoid use, phagocyte dysfunction (CGD, advanced HIV, relapsed leukemia) and underlying respiratory disease, with angioinvasion and hemorrhagic infarction; from the lungs (>80% of cases) it may disseminate hematogenously (most often to brain). Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in apparently immunocompetent hosts with prior lung disease and a suboptimal TH1-like inflammatory response. Allergic forms (ABPA, SAFS) reflect a TH2-like hypersensitivity response to A. fumigatus, classically complicating asthma and cystic fibrosis. Multiple gene variants underlie susceptibility to each form (Harrison 22e p.1713-1714).
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis (chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma classically mimic and follow TB)
Lung carcinoma (Aspergillus nodule may resemble early lung cancer)
Bacterial sinusitis (early invasive Aspergillus sinusitis not radiologically distinguishable)
Other angioinvasive molds, notably mucormycosis and Fusarium/Scedosporium (histologically can mimic Aspergillus)
infectionMimics: Mucormycosis (Mucorales) causing invasive pulmonary or sinus disease
Pulmonary tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease
nonInfectiousMimics: Lung carcinoma (Aspergillus nodule mimics early carcinoma)
COVID-19 itself (nodules with halo signs are a feature of COVID-19; invasive aspergillosis requires supportive evidence)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis / other cavitary lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Galactomannan antigen detection (respiratory sample more sensitive than serum; critical in ICU/ventilated patients)
Real-time PCR of respiratory samples and blood (and sputum PCR in chronic disease)
Aspergillus IgG antibody (chronic forms) and Aspergillus-specific IgE plus total IgE (allergic forms)
High-volume fungal culture on fungal media (also checks for azole resistance)
Microscopy/cytology and histopathology of affected tissue (hyaline narrow septate hyphae branching at 45 degrees)
Thoracic CT (halo sign, air-crescent, nodules, cavitation); MRI for cerebral and sinus disease
Bronchoscopy with tracheobronchial lavage; positron emission tomography for chronic cavitary disease and nodules
redFlags: Life-threatening / massive hemoptysis (the most significant complication of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and may be the presenting manifestation)
Neurologic deterioration: mood change, focal signs, seizures, declining mental status suggesting cerebral aspergillosis (hemorrhagic infarction/abscess)
Orbital apex syndrome (blindness and proptosis), facial swelling, cavernous sinus thrombosis or carotid occlusion in invasive/chronic sinusitis
Fever progressing despite glucocorticoids in an immunocompromised host
harrison.prognosis: Invasive aspergillosis is curable if immune reconstitution occurs, whereas allergic and chronic forms are not curable. Mortality of invasive aspergillosis is 30-70% if treated but ~100% if the diagnosis is missed; cerebral aspergillosis, Aspergillus endocarditis, bilateral extensive invasive pulmonary disease, late-stage AIDS, relapsed uncontrolled leukemia, and liver failure carry very poor outcomes. Untreated chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis causes clinical deterioration in ~70%; with antifungal treatment mortality is 15-20% in the first year, ~40% over 5 years, and 50-60% over 10 years, with treatment failure in ~30% (more with azole resistance). ABPA/SAFS respond to glucocorticoids and antifungals (~60% to itraconazole, ~80% to voriconazole/posaconazole) but relapse after discontinuation is common (Harrison 22e p.1717).
pitfalls: Requesting only bacterial culture rather than fungal culture may miss the diagnosis (bacterial agar is less sensitive); only 10-30% of invasive cases have a positive culture
Fluconazole is commonly used for prophylaxis but has NO activity against Aspergillus species
No prophylactic regimen is completely successful
Antifungal therapy reduces the sensitivity of antigen detection
Aspergillus IgG may not be positive on initial testing in subacute/nonneutropenic invasive disease
A positive respiratory culture may represent only noninvasive disease or airway colonization, not invasion
Contrast CT of the brain is often contraindicated by poor renal function and unenhanced CT is usually nonspecific; MRI is the most useful immediate investigation for cerebral disease
Surgery is problematic in chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and often causes serious complications; bronchial artery embolization is preferred for problematic hemoptysis
harrison.severityClassification: By disease category: INVASIVE (acute course <=1 month, subacute 1-3 months) - angioinvasive/nonangioinvasive/granulomatous pulmonary, invasive sinusitis, tracheobronchitis, disseminated, cerebral, endocarditis, cutaneous, keratitis/endophthalmitis. CHRONIC - chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis (destroyed lung), Aspergillus bronchitis, Aspergillus nodule, chronic invasive and chronic granulomatous sinusitis. SAPROPHYTIC - aspergilloma (single fungal ball), airway colonization, maxillary sinus fungal ball. ALLERGIC - ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization (SAFS), allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1714-1715).
management: Prompt antifungal therapy for invasive disease with a mould-active triazole such as voriconazole or isavuconazole first-line, with liposomal amphotericin B or an echinocandin as alternatives
Reversal of predisposing immunosuppression where possible, including reducing glucocorticoids and supporting neutrophil recovery in neutropenic hosts

Long-term oral triazole therapy (itraconazole or voriconazole) for chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, and oral corticosteroids with an antifungal, plus anti-IgE therapy such as omalizumab in selected patients, for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Surgical resection for symptomatic aspergilloma, localised chronic cavitary disease or life-threatening haemoptysis, with bronchial artery embolisation as an alternative for bleeding
Therapeutic drug monitoring of triazole levels, testing for azole resistance, and serial galactomannan to gauge response
Antifungal prophylaxis in the highest-risk immunocompromised patients, such as those with prolonged neutropenia or graft-versus-host disease
Multidisciplinary care and escalation for disseminated or cerebral disease, endocarditis or refractory infection
